name: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)
populations: people starting or returning to exercise
athletes at the start of a season or training block
people trying a new activity or exercise
recreational and elite athletes after eccentric or plyometric sessions
summary: Muscle pain and stiffness that peaks 1 to 3 days after unaccustomed, usually eccentric, exercise. It is self-limiting, a first bout protects later bouts, and most recovery strategies have small effects.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Peak soreness is reported at 48–72 hours; it usually settles within about a week (a common clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Light training can usually continue; reduce intensity and duration for 1–2 days after severe DOMS and re-introduce hard eccentric work progressively

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Diffuse muscle tenderness and pain on stretch or contraction 1–3 days after unaccustomed exercise, with no focal defect and a typical time course

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed. MRI shows increased T2 signal in damaged muscle, but imaging is kept for atypical or severe presentations

keyFacts.label: Risk factors
keyFacts.value: Eccentric or unaccustomed exercise, high intensity or duration, and the start of a season or return after a break

keyFacts.label: Recovery strategies
keyFacts.value: Small, short-lived or uncertain effects; stretching, electrical currents and ultrasound showed no useful effect

overview:
Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is muscle pain and stiffness that develops some hours after unaccustomed or eccentric exercise and peaks at about 48–72 h [r1]. It is regarded as a mild type of ultrastructural muscle injury, with reduced force capacity, painful restriction of movement, stiffness and swelling [r1]. Eccentric actions, in which the muscle lengthens under load, cause micro-injury more often and more severely than other contraction types, and the intensity and duration of the exercise also matter [r2]. DOMS is most common when athletes return to training after a period of reduced activity, and whenever a new type of activity is introduced [r2].

The mechanism is still incompletely understood. Six theories have been proposed (lactic acid, muscle spasm, connective tissue damage, muscle damage, inflammation and enzyme efflux), and an integration of two or more probably explains soreness [r2]. A 2026 systematic review concluded that DOMS cannot be explained by one biological mechanism and is better seen as a multifactorial neurophysiological response than as simply the result of muscle damage [r3]. DOMS is self-limiting. One bout of eccentric exercise protects against damage from later bouts (the repeated-bout effect), although a unified explanation of that protection is also still lacking [r4]. Many popular recovery strategies have small, short-lived or uncertain effects, and some have no demonstrable effect [r5,r6,r7]. The physiotherapist confirms the diagnosis, excludes more serious conditions such as exertional rhabdomyolysis, reassures, and guides sensible load and recovery choices.

epidemiology.text: DOMS is most prevalent at the beginning of the sporting season, when athletes return to training after a period of reduced activity, and whenever athletes are first introduced to certain activities, regardless of the time of year [r2]. Eccentric activities induce micro-injury at a greater frequency and severity than other types of muscle action, and exercise intensity and duration are also important [r2]. The size of the response depends on the type of eccentric exercise: circulating neutrophil counts and systemic cytokine responses are greater after eccentric exercise that uses a large muscle mass (for example downhill running or eccentric cycling) than after eccentric exercise of a smaller muscle mass [r8]. Responses also differ with age and sex. Leukocyte and cytokine responses are impaired in elderly people, and cellular infiltration into muscle is greater in human females than males after eccentric exercise [r8]. Whether men and women differ in muscle damage is contested: animal studies show that females experience less damage, whereas human studies suggest either no difference or that women are more prone to damage [r9]. No population incidence figure for DOMS was identified in the sources reviewed, so none is quoted.

intrinsic: No recent exposure to the specific eccentric task, which means the protective repeated-bout adaptation is absent [r4,r9]
Sex and age: responses of the inflammatory system differ with age and sex, but the effect on soreness itself is contested or uncertain [r8,r9]
Individual neurophysiological responses vary, which affects symptoms and the response to recovery strategies [r3]
Deconditioning after a layoff, which leaves the muscle less prepared for the task [r2]
extrinsic: Eccentric and unaccustomed exercise such as downhill running, lowering phases of lifts, plyometrics and a new activity [r2]
High exercise intensity and long duration [r2]
Start of the sporting season or a return from a break; modifiable by introducing eccentric or novel activities progressively over 1–2 weeks [r2]
Exercise using a large muscle mass, which produces larger systemic inflammatory responses [r8]

mechanism.summary: DOMS follows exercise that loads muscle in a way it is not used to, most reliably eccentric work: the muscle produces force while it is being lengthened, as in the lowering phase of a squat, downhill running, landings or a first session of resistance training [r2]. The leading model is initial mechanical disruption of sarcomeres, followed by impaired excitation–contraction coupling and calcium signalling, and then activation of calcium-sensitive degradation pathways [r8]. The exact pathway is unknown [r1]. Soreness appears hours later and peaks at 48–72 h because it depends on a sequence of local and systemic responses, not just on the initial damage [r1].
sequence: The person performs unaccustomed exercise, with a large eccentric component (slow lowering, downhill running, landing or a new exercise) [r2].
The active muscle is lengthened under load, so a limited number of active fibres carry high force at long muscle lengths (mechanistic model).
Sarcomeres are mechanically disrupted, and Z-line streaming can be seen under the microscope [r9,r8].
Excitation–contraction coupling and calcium signalling are impaired, and calcium-sensitive degradation pathways are activated [r8].
Inflammatory cells infiltrate the muscle and cytokines are released; nociceptors become sensitised, and in humans nerve growth factor (NGF) rises in the muscle after a first eccentric bout [r8,r10].
Soreness, stiffness, swelling and loss of force develop over the next day, with peak soreness reported at 48–72 h [r1].
The muscle repairs and adapts over days, and a repeated-bout effect protects it against the next similar bout [r4].

variants.name: Eccentric resistance exercise
variants.description: Slow lowering, Nordic-type or first-time resistance sessions. A 2026 narrative synthesis proposed that resistance exercise produces strength loss with group III and IV nociceptor activation [r3].

variants.name: Downhill running and endurance exercise
variants.description: Large muscle mass and many repeated contractions. Endurance exercise was proposed to give cumulative inflammatory responses, with IL-6 increasing within 48 h [r3,r8].

variants.name: Plyometric and landing exercise
variants.description: Jumping and landing loads. In the same synthesis plyometric exercise was proposed to disrupt proprioceptive control alongside C-fibre sensitisation; these distinctions are proposals, not settled facts [r3].

variants.name: Second bout (repeated-bout effect)
variants.description: After a first damaging bout, a similar bout produces much less soreness. In a small study of seven adults, peak DOMS was more than twice as great after the first bout of one-leg eccentric cycling as after the second [r10,r4].

anatomy.text: A muscle is a hierarchy: sarcomeres in series form myofibrils, fibres are wrapped in endomysium and bundled by perimysium within the epimysium, and the muscle transmits force to bone through the muscle–tendon junction and tendon. DOMS involves the fibres and their sarcomeres, the surrounding connective tissue and the sensory nerve endings in the muscle. Connective tissue damage is one of the six proposed theories [r2]. Sensitised group III and IV nociceptors carry the pain signal [r3].

structures.name: Muscle fibres and sarcomeres
structures.role: The contractile units. Initial mechanical disruption of sarcomeres, with Z-line streaming, is the first step in the leading damage model [r9,r8]

structures.name: Connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium)
structures.role: Transmits force around and between fibres; connective tissue damage is one of six proposed mechanisms of DOMS [r2]

structures.name: Muscle–tendon junction and tendon
structures.role: Transmit muscle force to bone. In DOMS the change is diffuse within the muscle, in contrast to the focal junctional injury of a strain (clinical contrast)

structures.name: Sensory nerve endings (group III and IV afferents)
structures.role: Nociceptors that become sensitised and carry the soreness signal; NGF rose in human muscle 24 h after a first eccentric bout [r3,r10]

structures.name: Intramuscular blood vessels and interstitium
structures.role: Deliver leukocytes and remove debris; leukocyte infiltration and local cytokine production follow eccentric damage [r8]

structures.name: Satellite cells
structures.role: Muscle stem cells that support the repair pathways after eccentric damage [r11]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Eccentric exercise causes exercise-induced muscle damage. Direct measures of damage include cellular and subcellular disturbances, particularly Z-line streaming, and indirect markers include increased T2 signal on MRI, prolonged loss of force, inflammatory markers in muscle and blood, muscle proteins in the blood, and soreness [r9]. The initial injury is ascribed to mechanical disruption of the fibre, and subsequent damage is linked to inflammatory processes and to changes in excitation–contraction coupling [r9]. A sequence of mechanical disruption of sarcomeres, impaired excitation–contraction coupling and calcium signalling, and activation of calcium-sensitive degradation pathways has been proposed [r8]. The molecular basis of soreness itself is relatively poorly understood [r12].

Soreness is not simply a readout of damage. DOMS is thought to be at least partly mechanical hyperalgesia from nociceptor sensitisation, driven in animals by NGF and GDNF; in seven adults, NGF mRNA in vastus lateralis was higher 24 h after a first bout of eccentric cycling than after the second, which paralleled the repeated-bout effect on soreness [r10]. That is a very small human study. The 2026 review concluded that DOMS cannot be explained by one mechanism, and that different exercise types activate overlapping but different combinations of inflammatory, neural, metabolic and proprioceptive pathways [r3]. The clinical picture of reduced range of motion, shock attenuation and peak torque, and altered muscle recruitment, can place unaccustomed stress on other tissues if training resumes too early [r2].

structures.name: Sarcomeres and muscle fibres
structures.effect: Mechanical disruption, Z-line streaming and loss of force-generating capacity [r9,r8]

structures.name: Excitation–contraction coupling and calcium handling
structures.effect: Impaired coupling and calcium signalling, then calcium-sensitive degradation [r8]

structures.name: Connective tissue
structures.effect: May be disturbed as part of the damage and contributes to stiffness and tenderness (one of the proposed theories) [r2]

structures.name: Muscle–tendon junction and tendon
structures.effect: Not torn: a tendon or junctional tear is a different injury, and should be considered if the pain is focal and sudden (clinical contrast)

muscles.name: The exercised muscle (for example the quadriceps)
muscles.effect: Loses force-generating capacity; in a small study, knee-extensor isometric torque at 48 h was about 20% lower after the first eccentric bout than after the second [r10]. Range of motion, shock attenuation and peak torque fall [r2].

muscles.name: Synergists and the kinetic chain
muscles.effect: Altered muscle sequencing and recruitment can place unaccustomed stress on muscles, ligaments and tendons, which may raise the risk of a further injury if a premature return to sport is attempted [r2].

muscles.name: Muscle after repeated exposure
muscles.effect: Becomes less vulnerable. Proposed contributors are altered motor unit recruitment, sarcomeres added in series, a blunted inflammatory response and fewer stress-susceptible fibres, but there is no general agreement on the cause [r9,r4].

cellular.description: Sarcomeres are disrupted under high force at long muscle lengths, with Z-line streaming [r9,r8].
Impaired excitation–contraction coupling and calcium signalling activate calcium-sensitive degradation pathways [r8].
Leukocytes infiltrate the muscle, cytokines are produced, and nociceptors become sensitised; NGF was raised at 24 h after a first bout in a small human study [r8,r10].
Peak soreness is reported at 48–72 h, with stiffness, swelling and reduced force [r1].

The muscle repairs, with satellite cell-mediated and alternative repair pathways [r11]; adaptation reduces damage from the next bout (repeated-bout effect) [r4]. The time course of full recovery is not well quantified in the sources read.

systems.effect: Peripheral sensitisation of group III and IV nociceptors and, in animals, NGF- and GDNF-driven mechanical hyperalgesia; proprioception can be disturbed, particularly after plyometric exercise [r3,r10].

Leukocyte infiltration, local and systemic cytokine release, and raised systemic markers such as IL-6 within 48 h of endurance exercise [r8,r3]. The size of the response depends on the muscle mass used, the number of bouts, age and sex [r8].
Reduced range of motion, shock attenuation and peak torque, with altered recruitment patterns that shift load to other tissues [r2].
Muscle proteins and enzymes such as creatine kinase appear in the blood [r9]. These are indirect markers of damage, and biomarkers of muscle damage have been described as flawed [r11].
Expecting soreness, or fearing it, may change how people train and rest (clinical observation, not established in the sources read). Reassurance about the benign course is helpful.

timeframes.summary: Soreness is reported to peak at 48–72 h [r1]. Most people settle within about a week and return to usual training, although this range is a common clinical convention and was not quantified in the sources read. The time course varies with the exercise, the muscle mass and prior exposure [r8].

healing.description: Soreness, stiffness and loss of force develop over the hours after unaccustomed exercise
Peak soreness is reported at 48–72 h, with reduced range of motion, tenderness and weakness [r1,r2]
Soreness fades over the following days (typical clinical course; a common clinical convention)
Force and range of motion return and the muscle adapts, so the next bout is better tolerated (repeated-bout effect) [r4]

milestones.label: Soreness developing
milestones.note: Begins hours after the exercise and builds

milestones.label: Soreness largely settled
milestones.note: Typical clinical course; a common clinical convention

milestones.label: Usual training resumed
milestones.note: Criteria-based: soreness and strength, not the calendar

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. Light training can continue; athletes who train daily should reduce intensity and duration for 1–2 days after intense DOMS-inducing exercise, or train less affected body parts [r2]. Full-intensity and eccentric work resumes once soreness and strength have returned to near normal.

symptoms: Muscle ache, tenderness and stiffness that begin hours after unaccustomed or eccentric exercise and build over 1–3 days [r1]
Pain on stretching, contracting, squatting or walking down stairs when the leg muscles are involved
A feeling of weakness or heaviness in the muscle, and a reluctance to use it
Both sides affected if both were exercised, often symmetrical and diffuse rather than sharply localised
Gradual improvement over several days, with no night pain or constant pain
signs: Diffuse tenderness through the muscle belly on palpation, without a focal defect or gap
Reduced range of motion and stiffness, and pain on passive stretch of the involved muscle [r2]
Reduced force on resisted testing, usually painful rather than truly weak [r2]
Mild swelling or a firm, tight feeling in the muscle in more severe cases [r1]
Normal neurological examination, normal pulses, no marked bruising and no calf asymmetry

subjective: Exercise exposure: what was done, how new it was, eccentric content (downhill, lowering, landings), intensity and duration [r2]
Time course: onset hours after exercise, rising over 1–3 days, and whether it is now settling [r1]
Symptom pattern: diffuse aching in the exercised muscles, usually both sides, with no focal sharp pain at the time of exercise
Red-flag screen: dark or 'cola' urine, severe swelling, pain out of proportion, weakness, or numbness; recent heat exposure, infection, drugs or alcohol, supplements or medication [r13,r14]
Training history and plans: last similar session, competition dates, and what recovery strategies have been tried
Medications that affect muscle, such as statins, and any prior episode of unusually severe or prolonged soreness (clinical reasoning)
observation: Guarded gait, difficulty with stairs, and reluctance to squat or sit down and stand up
Symmetrical swelling or fullness in the exercised muscles, if present
Absence of focal bruising, a visible defect, or marked asymmetry of the calf or thigh
palpation: Diffuse tenderness through the muscle belly, compared with the other side; maximal tenderness often near the muscle–tendon junction (clinical observation)
No palpable gap or lump, which would suggest a strain or haematoma rather than DOMS
Compartment feel: soft and compressible. A tense, hard compartment suggests compartment syndrome or severe damage (clinical reasoning)
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive range of the joints crossed by the sore muscle, which is often reduced and painful at end range [r2]
Compare with the other side and with the person's usual flexibility
strength: Resisted contraction of the muscle, noting pain and weakness; force is reduced after eccentric exercise [r2]
Dynamometry or repeated sit-to-stand if available, which gives a baseline for tracking recovery [r10]
neuro: Sensation, reflexes and distal power are normal in DOMS. Any numbness, paraesthesia or true motor weakness needs a different explanation, such as a compartment syndrome or nerve injury [r14]
functional: Bodyweight squat, stair descent and gait: pain should ease with repetition, and the movement should still be possible
A short, easy walk or cycle to see whether warming up reduces the pain, which is typical of DOMS and temporary [r2]

specialTests.name: Muscle belly palpation with comparison
specialTests.purpose: Distinguish diffuse DOMS tenderness from the focal tenderness or gap of a muscle strain
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the length of the affected muscle with the muscle relaxed, then compare with the other side and across the muscle–tendon junction.
specialTests.positive: Diffuse tenderness without a defect fits DOMS. A focal, sharp tender point with a palpable gap suggests a strain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Resisted contraction and passive stretch of the affected muscle
specialTests.purpose: Show the typical painful stretch and painful contraction pattern, and look for weakness out of proportion to pain
specialTests.procedure: Test resisted isometric contraction at mid-range, then passively stretch the muscle to end range, and compare sides.
specialTests.positive: Pain on both stretch and contraction, with force reduced mainly by pain, fits DOMS. Marked weakness or a visible defect needs further assessment. No accuracy figures were identified.

specialTests.name: Compartment and calf screen
specialTests.purpose: Exclude acute compartment syndrome and deep vein thrombosis as the cause of severe pain or swelling
specialTests.procedure: Palpate for a tense, hard compartment, check pain with passive stretch, sensation and distal pulses, and look for unilateral calf swelling and tenderness.
specialTests.positive: A tense, hard compartment, pain out of proportion, neurological change, or unilateral swelling needs urgent medical review. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

clinicalRules.name: No validated clinical prediction rule
clinicalRules.description: Diagnosis is clinical: a typical exercise exposure, a delayed and diffuse pattern, and a normal screen for red flags. Time course and context are the key features [r1,r2].

clinicalRules.name: Red-flag triage for rhabdomyolysis
clinicalRules.description: Dark 'cola' urine, marked swelling and weakness with muscle pain after strenuous exercise should be treated as possible exertional rhabdomyolysis, which can cause acute renal failure, electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias [r13].

outcomeMeasures.name: Soreness rating (0–10 numeric scale or 100 mm visual analogue scale) at rest, on movement and on palpation
outcomeMeasures.use: Tracks the time course. Soreness and torque were measured at 24 and 48 h in a recent eccentric-exercise study [r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: Range of motion (goniometer or inclinometer)
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective measure of stiffness, which falls after eccentric exercise [r2]

outcomeMeasures.name: Maximal voluntary contraction (dynamometry) or repeated sit-to-stand
outcomeMeasures.use: Tracks force recovery; muscle force is reduced for days after damaging exercise [r9,r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pressure pain threshold
outcomeMeasures.use: Quantifies tenderness for research and for repeated bedside comparison (clinical convention; accuracy not established in the sources read)

outcomeMeasures.name: Creatine kinase (research and medical use only)
outcomeMeasures.use: A marker of muscle protein release. CK is an imperfect measure of damage, and it is measured when rhabdomyolysis is suspected [r9,r11]

imaging.indication: Typical exposure, delayed diffuse soreness and a normal examination
Atypical, severe or prolonged pain, suspected strain or other muscle injury
imaging.findings: Increased T2 signal intensity in damaged muscle is one of the indirect markers of exercise-induced damage [r9]

imaging.indication: Suspected focal strain, haematoma or collection, and to guide further care
imaging.findings: Focal disruption or a collection points away from DOMS (clinical convention)

differentials.name: Acute muscle strain
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset during exercise with sharp, focal pain, a tender point or gap and bruising. DOMS is diffuse and delayed.

differentials.name: Exertional rhabdomyolysis
differentials.distinguishing: Severe pain, marked swelling and weakness, and sometimes dark 'cola' urine, with very high CK; can lead to renal failure [r13]. Needs urgent medical assessment.

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Pain out of proportion, a tense compartment, pain on passive stretch and neurological change (classic features). It can follow a strenuous workout, and delayed diagnosis risks irreversible muscle and nerve damage [r14].

differentials.name: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Reproducible tightness and pain at a given exercise intensity that settles with rest, rather than a delayed, diffuse ache that peaks at 48–72 h.

differentials.name: Bone stress injury
differentials.distinguishing: Focal bony tenderness with load-related pain that worsens across weeks; soreness is not delayed by a day but follows a load-time pattern.

differentials.name: Deep vein thrombosis
differentials.distinguishing: Unilateral calf pain and swelling, warmth and risk factors, without a relevant exercise exposure; requires medical assessment (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Statin-associated or other drug or viral myalgia
differentials.distinguishing: Widespread aching and weakness without an obvious eccentric exposure, or a viral illness; review medications and arrange medical assessment (clinical reasoning).

redFlags: Dark ('cola'-coloured) urine, marked swelling, severe pain or weakness after strenuous exercise: suspect exertional rhabdomyolysis, which can cause acute renal failure, electrolyte abnormalities and arrhythmias. Send for same-day medical assessment [r13].

Pain out of proportion, a tense or hard muscle compartment, pain on passive stretch, numbness or foot or hand weakness after strenuous exercise: suspect acute exertional compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency with a risk of irreversible muscle and nerve damage. Send to emergency [r14].

Soreness that gets worse after 3–4 days, does not settle after about 1–2 weeks, or recurs with minimal exercise: look for another cause (strain, bone stress injury, myopathy, drugs) and consider medical review (clinical convention).
Unilateral calf pain, swelling or warmth with risk factors, or breathlessness or chest pain: exclude deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism with urgent medical assessment (clinical convention).
Repeated episodes of severe soreness with minimal exercise, or a family history of muscle disease or sickle cell trait: consider metabolic or genetic muscle conditions and medical review [r13].

management.principles: DOMS is self-limiting, so management is reassurance, sensible load and comfort measures, not a search for a cure. Gentle activity relieves pain temporarily, and exercise is the most effective way of alleviating pain during DOMS, although the analgesic effect is also temporary [r2]. Athletes who train daily should reduce intensity and duration for 1–2 days after intense DOMS-inducing exercise, or work less affected body parts [r2]. The evidence for every recovery strategy is of low to moderate quality, effects are small and short-lived, and several strategies have no effect, so choose on cost, safety and preference, and do not oversell them [r5,r2]. The best intervention is prevention: introduce eccentric or novel exercise progressively [r2], which uses the protective repeated-bout effect [r4].

medical.name: Medical review to exclude rhabdomyolysis or compartment syndrome
medical.description: For dark urine, marked swelling, pain out of proportion or neurological change: same-day assessment, with CK and renal function, and emergency care for suspected compartment syndrome [r13,r14].

medical.name: Simple analgesia (for example paracetamol) for comfort
medical.description: Short-term simple analgesia may help comfort and sleep when soreness is severe. No trial evidence was found in the sources reviewed; keep to standard doses.

medical.name: NSAIDs (prophylactic or treatment)
medical.description: A 2003 review reported dose-dependent effects that may depend on timing [r2]. In a randomised, double-blind, cross-over study of 12 adults, a single prophylactic dose of ibuprofen (800 mg), flurbiprofen (100 mg) or celecoxib (200 mg) did not reduce soreness after a plyometric session, and ibuprofen and flurbiprofen did not prevent loss of force [r15]. Anti-inflammatory drugs largely did not alter inflammatory responses to eccentric exercise [r8]. Not a routine strategy.

medical.name: Whole-body cryotherapy (extreme cold air)
medical.description: A Cochrane review of four small trials (64 people) found very low-quality evidence and could not tell whether it reduces soreness; adverse events were not monitored [r7].

physio.name: Education, reassurance and expected course
physio.description: Explain that DOMS is a benign, self-limiting response to unaccustomed or eccentric exercise, peaks at about 48–72 h, and settles; explain that the next similar bout will be better tolerated (repeated-bout effect) [r1,r4].

physio.name: Light activity and active recovery (relative rest of the sore muscle)
physio.description: Easy walking, cycling or work on less affected body parts. Exercise relieves the pain temporarily [r2]. Active recovery was one of the techniques with a small to large decrease in DOMS in a meta-analysis of 99 studies (g between −2.26 and −0.40 across the effective methods) [r5].

physio.name: Massage
physio.description: In a meta-analysis of 29 studies (1012 participants), massage did not improve strength, jump, sprint, endurance or fatigue, but was associated with small but statistically significant improvements in DOMS and flexibility [r16]. A meta-analysis of 99 studies found massage to be the most powerful technique for reducing DOMS and fatigue [r5]. Effects are small and the quality of the contributing trials varies; the timing and technique of application matter [r2].

physio.name: Compression garments
physio.description: A meta-analysis of 12 studies found a moderate effect on DOMS (Hedges' g 0.403, 95% CI 0.236–0.569) [r17]. Another meta-analysis found a reduction in perceptual measures (SMD −0.43, 15 studies), no effect on CK, and high heterogeneity, and said the findings need corroboration [r18].

physio.name: Cold-water immersion
physio.description: A Cochrane review of 17 small, low-quality trials (366 participants) found less soreness than passive recovery at 24 h (SMD −0.55), 48 h (−0.66), 72 h (−0.93) and 96 h (−0.58), with heterogeneous results; most trials did not monitor adverse events [r19]. It may relieve discomfort in the short term.

physio.name: Foam rolling
physio.description: A 2026 systematic review reported a small effect on DOMS (SMD −0.34), but most studies lacked extractable effect sizes, so a full meta-analysis was not possible [r3]. Low cost and low risk.

physio.name: Progressive exposure to eccentric or novel exercise
physio.description: Introduce eccentric exercise or new activities progressively over 1–2 weeks at the start of or during the season to reduce physical impairment and training disruption [r2]. One bout of eccentric exercise protects against damage from later bouts [r4]. The optimal dose of a 'priming' bout is not established.

physio.name: Stretching before or after exercise
physio.description: A Cochrane review of 12 studies found that stretching before, after or both did not produce clinically important reductions in DOMS; pooled reductions at one day were about 0.5 and 1 point on a 100-point scale, and a large field trial of 2377 people found a 3.8-point reduction in peak soreness over a week, which is very small [r6].

physio.name: Therapeutic ultrasound, electrical currents, homeopathy
physio.description: A 2003 review found no effect of ultrasound, electrical current modalities or homeopathy on soreness [r2]. A 2018 meta-analysis found no change in DOMS for the methods outside its list of effective techniques; its search covered electrostimulation and stretching [r5].

physio.name: Returning at once to maximal eccentric or high-intensity work
physio.description: Compensatory recruitment patterns may increase the risk of further injury if a premature return to sport is attempted [r2].

education: DOMS is a normal, harmless response to unfamiliar exercise. It builds over a day, peaks at about 2–3 days and settles within about a week.
Gentle movement helps you feel better for a while, but does not speed up the underlying repair. Complete rest is not needed.
No recovery product or method has been shown to reliably cut soreness by a large amount; massage, compression and cold water may help a little. Stretching does not prevent or treat DOMS.
The next time you do the same exercise it will be much less sore, so start new or eccentric exercise gently and build up over 1–2 weeks.
See a doctor the same day if you have dark urine, severe swelling, pain out of proportion, numbness, or weakness after hard exercise.

rehab.overview: DOMS needs a short, criteria-based return to normal training, not a rehabilitation programme. The stages are: settle with light activity, resume usual training at a reduced load, and build tolerance to eccentric load so the next bout is less damaging. Stage timeframes are typical and criteria override the calendar. The key points from the evidence are that gentle exercise relieves pain temporarily, that intensity and duration should be reduced for 1–2 days after severe DOMS, and that eccentric exercise should be introduced progressively over 1–2 weeks [r2]. Doses below are common clinical conventions, not trial-based prescriptions.

stages.name: Settle & stay moving
goals: Reassure and set the expectation of recovery
Avoid further heavy eccentric loading of the sore muscle
precautions: Reduce intensity and duration for 1–2 days after intense DOMS-inducing exercise [r2]
Do not force through sharp, focal or worsening pain; stop and reassess
Screen red flags (dark urine, severe swelling, neurological change) before exercising [r13]

exercises.name: Easy walking
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, once or twice a day, at a conversational pace (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Smooth, relaxed steps; the soreness usually eases as the muscle warms up

exercises.name: Easy cycling or pool walking
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min at low resistance, daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Keep the effort light; no resisted or downhill work

exercises.name: Gentle active range of motion (heel slides)
exercises.cues: Move smoothly through the pain-free range

exercises.name: Foam rolling or self-massage of the sore muscle
exercises.dosage: 1–2 min per muscle, once or twice a day, light to moderate pressure (optional; small, uncertain effect)
exercises.cues: Keep the pressure tolerable; avoid bony areas

exercises.name: Train less affected body parts
exercises.dosage: Usual upper-body or core session at normal intensity [r2]
exercises.cues: Choose exercises that do not load the sore muscle

progressionCriteria: Soreness at rest at or below 2/10 and improving day by day
Can walk and use stairs without a limp
Range of motion within about 80–90% of the other side or of normal (clinical convention)

stages.name: Resume usual training
goals: Return to usual aerobic and strength sessions at a modestly reduced load
precautions: Keep eccentric and plyometric content low until soreness and strength have returned to near normal
Stop and review if soreness gets worse on day 4 or later, or red flags appear
Soreness during the session at or below about 3/10 and settled by the next day (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Usual aerobic session at reduced duration
exercises.dosage: 70–80% of the usual duration, flat terrain, 3–5 times a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Avoid downhill running and hard decelerations for now

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels; control rather than depth

exercises.name: Bodyweight squat to a comfortable depth
exercises.cues: Pain-free range; sit back and keep the heels down

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Smooth tempo, full range as comfort allows

exercises.name: Dynamic mobility and light stretching for comfort
exercises.dosage: 5–10 min, daily (for comfort only, not to prevent soreness) [r6]
exercises.cues: Gentle; do not stretch into pain

progressionCriteria: Soreness at or below 2/10 with daily activity and at or below 3/10 during exercise
Strength within about 90% of the other side or of baseline on a simple test (clinical convention)
Stairs and squat pain-free or nearly so

stages.name: Build eccentric tolerance
goals: Re-introduce eccentric loading gradually over 1–2 weeks [r2]
Use the repeated-bout effect to protect against future soreness
Return to full training with no disruption
precautions: Add eccentric volume gradually; increase by about 10–20% a week (clinical convention)
Expect mild soreness after a new stimulus; it should be milder and shorter than the first time [r4]
Stop and review if soreness is severe or red flags appear

exercises.name: Tempo squat
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8, 3 s lowering, light load, twice a week, increasing the load over 2 weeks
exercises.cues: Control the lowering and drive up smoothly

exercises.name: Slow step-down
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 8 each leg, 3 s lowering, twice a week
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring lowering (partial range first)
exercises.dosage: 2 × 3–5, building by 1–2 repetitions a week over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Lean forward from the knees as slowly as you can

exercises.name: Gradual downhill walking, then jogging
exercises.dosage: Start with 5–10 min on a gentle slope and build by about 10% a week (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Short, quick steps and a soft landing

exercises.name: Low-height landing practice
exercises.dosage: 2 × 5 soft landings, twice a week, then increase height gradually
exercises.cues: Bend the hips and knees and land softly

progressionCriteria: Eccentric session produces only mild, short soreness (at or below 3/10 for no more than 1–2 days) (clinical convention)
Full training volume tolerated for at least 1–2 weeks
Strength and range symmetrical and pain-free

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria exist for DOMS. The criteria below reflect clinical practice and the principle that premature return can increase the risk of further injury [r2]
Resting soreness at or below 2/10, with pain on palpation and movement at or below about 2–3/10 (clinical convention)
Range of motion and force at or near the other side or personal baseline (clinical convention)
Normal movement patterns on squat, step-down and gait, without compensatory recruitment [r2]
Training load and eccentric content re-introduced progressively over 1–2 weeks [r2]
No red flags (dark urine, severe swelling, neurological change)
tests: Soreness rating at rest, on palpation and on movement
Range of motion compared with the other side
Dynamometry or repeated sit-to-stand compared with baseline or the other side
Next-day soreness after a trial session

prognosis: DOMS is self-limiting. Peak soreness is reported at 48–72 h and it settles over the following days, although the time to complete recovery of force is not well quantified in the sources reviewed [r1]. A repeated-bout effect reduces the response to later bouts: in a small study of seven adults, peak DOMS was more than twice as great after the first bout as after the second, although the mechanism of this adaptation remains unresolved [r10,r4]. The main risks are a premature return to full training, when altered recruitment patterns can place unaccustomed stress on muscles, ligaments and tendons [r2], and the rare severe presentations (exertional rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome) that should be recognised early [r13,r14].
prevention: Introduce eccentric exercise and new activities progressively over 1–2 weeks, particularly at the start of or during a season or after a break [r2].
Use the repeated-bout effect: a previous bout of eccentric exercise protects against damage from later bouts, although the best dose of a priming bout is not established [r4,r10].
Match training load to current conditioning, especially for large-muscle-mass work such as downhill running or eccentric cycling [r8].
Do not rely on stretching, ultrasound or electrical modalities to prevent soreness; they have not been shown to work [r6,r2].
Do not rely on prophylactic NSAIDs, which did not reduce soreness in a randomised cross-over study [r15].
Plan new or heavy eccentric sessions away from competition or key sessions, and consider reducing the intensity and duration of the next session after severe DOMS [r2].
clinicalPearls: A delayed, diffuse, symmetrical ache that peaks at 48–72 h after unfamiliar exercise is DOMS. A sudden, focal, sharp pain during exercise is a strain until proven otherwise [r1].

Pain out of proportion, a tense compartment, numbness or weakness after hard exercise is not DOMS. Treat it as compartment syndrome until excluded [r14]. Dark urine means exertional rhabdomyolysis until excluded [r13].

Be honest about recovery products. Massage had the largest effect in a 99-study meta-analysis but the effects are small, and stretching did not produce clinically important reductions in soreness in the Cochrane review [r5,r6].
Gentle exercise gives temporary relief, so a short easy walk is a useful test and a useful treatment [r2].
Next time will hurt less. Explain the repeated-bout effect, and use it by introducing eccentric work gradually [r4,r2].

Soreness and creatine kinase are indirect markers of muscle damage, and muscle-damage biomarkers have been described as flawed, so neither is a precise measure of how much damage has occurred [r9,r11].

forces.label: Slow lowering: quadriceps lengthen under load

captions.text: A person starts an unfamiliar session with plenty of slow, controlled lowering.
On the way down the quadriceps work while they are being lengthened: an eccentric contraction.
Eccentric loading damages muscle more often and more severely than other contractions.
Repeated lowering of an unaccustomed muscle is the classic trigger for DOMS.
There is little pain during the session. The soreness comes later.
Zooming into the working muscle.

actions.text: Micro-damage in the fibres, not a tear
Tendon intact: this is not a rupture

captions.text: The muscle belly does the work in a lowering contraction.
The load stretches the muscle while it is actively contracting.
Fibres are lengthened under high force, and the sarcomeres are mechanically strained.
The result is micro-damage within the fibres. The mechanism of soreness is not fully understood.
Over the next day the muscle swells, inflammatory cells arrive and nerve endings become sensitised.
Soreness and stiffness peak at about 48 to 72 hours.
No structure is torn. It settles over days, and the next bout is better tolerated.
Healthy muscle: ordered sarcomeres, with actin and myosin overlapping.
Contraction: the sarcomeres shorten as the muscle produces force.
Eccentric overstretch: the muscle is forced to lengthen while active, and the weakest sarcomeres are overstretched.
Sarcomere disruption: sarcomeres are mechanically disrupted and the Z-lines become irregular.
Inflammation: immune cells infiltrate, signalling molecules rise and nociceptors become sensitised.
Satellite cells activate to support repair of the damaged fibres.
Regeneration: the fibres recover, and the muscle adapts so the next bout does less damage.
